section.title: Nimit Sohoni: Quant Finance vs AI Research, PhDs, and Startup Careers
section.deck: Nimit Sohoni compares quant finance and AI research careers, explains when a PhD helps, and describes working at Cartesia, a voice AI startup.

blocks.text: The host introduces Nimit Sohoni as a Stanford PhD and former Citadel quant who now works at Cartesia, a voice AI company. In Nimit's view, a PhD opens doors in both AI research and quant finance but is not required. Strong math and computer science fundamentals carry across both fields. The skill a PhD really builds is research taste: picking problems that matter and can be solved. Nimit says quant work usually offers better work-life balance than AI research, while quant pay is opaque and firms are more secretive. The conversation ends with advice for technical people moving into AI research: build fundamentals, read widely, and show evidence of the skill through school or a startup.
blocks.heading: Nimit Sohoni's view: fundamentals and problem taste matter more than credentials

blocks.question: Which career opportunities are hard to reach without a PhD?
answer: Nimit says few opportunities are closed to people without a PhD, but a PhD makes some much easier. Academia requires one. Industry AI research and quantitative finance are the two areas where Nimit has seen a PhD open doors. Nimit adds that industry research in computer science and math is increasingly converging on AI.

followups.question: Does a PhD help at the first filter, or later in the hiring process?
answer: Both, according to Nimit. An interview is easier to get when a candidate has differentiated themselves, and a PhD can do that. Applying to a top AI firm without the usual school, internship, or connection signals is harder but still possible.
A PhD also builds a skill set that helps later on. Learning on the job, without a PhD, is another route that works for many people.
followups.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

followups.question: Would the role itself change with a PhD versus without one?
answer: Yes. Engineering-heavy AI work, such as training or evaluation infrastructure and data processing, does not need a PhD. More speculative architecture design can benefit from one, because a PhD gives time to explore directions that may not pay off soon.

A PhD is not necessary for someone whose only goal is to become an AI researcher. For someone still exploring and looking for problems that interest them, Nimit says a PhD can be a good way to do that.
followups.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.question: What skill set does a PhD develop?
answer: Nimit says the main skill is finding the right problems, which Nimit puts at about 90 percent of research. A researcher must find a problem that is interesting and meaningful, sometimes persuade others it matters, and scope it so it is tractable. Execution was Nimit's strength before the PhD. Research taste and problem selection were the big lessons, and they come from immersion in the field, through reading enough papers and talking with enough people.

followups.question: What tips help a researcher find the right problems?
answer: Nimit says the main habit is keeping up with the literature by reading as many papers as possible. Full reading is not needed. Skimming abstracts shows what people are thinking about.

Nimit also recommends working up gradually. Early on, a researcher should attack small sub-problems, such as extending a method to a special case. As they mature, they can take on bigger problems and new ideas. Skipping these steps is generally inadvisable.
followups.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.question: Where do you get your feed of hot research papers?
answer: Nimit says X is the main source, with talking to co-workers as a second. Nimit curates the feed so it is mostly machine learning papers.

To start, Nimit followed people from Stanford, professors whose papers Nimit had read, and prominent researchers at large labs. When a followed account shares an interesting paper, Nimit follows the authors tagged in it, so the list grew on its own.
blocks.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.question: Where were you in your career, and why did you become a quant?
answer: Nimit joined Citadel Securities after the PhD, having interned there just before graduating. By then Nimit had spent four to five years in AI research. Nimit had considered three careers that fit an interest in math and computation: machine learning research, quantitative finance, and quantum computing, which Nimit had no experience in.

Friends who had interned at Citadel Securities and other quant firms said they enjoyed it, and Nimit was curious. Nimit liked the work. It felt refreshing after a PhD that Nimit describes as a grind that can cause burnout, because the problems and environment were new.
blocks.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.question: Is the work culture at quant firms as intense as its reputation suggests?
answer: Nimit says the reputation is real in some places but varies by team and firm. Nimit personally had a good work-life balance as a quant.

Nimit links this partly to trading hours. US traders work around US market hours, plus a little time before and after, and the office culture follows that schedule. People cluster their work around those hours and rarely take work home, even though the work could be done at any time.
blocks.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.question: How would you describe quant work day to day?
answer: Nimit says it depends on the team, the sector, and the firm. A hedge fund and a market maker can have very different problems, and front-office and back-office quants do different jobs. Some quants focus on alpha, meaning they generate and backtest trading strategies and put them into practice. Others focus on monetizing strategies or on risk, building metrics that reduce risk without cutting profit. Some do data analysis on large sets of historical trade data.
Nimit says a strong math background is the common thread across these roles.

followups.question: How does math play a concrete role in the day-to-day work?
answer: Nimit says stochastic calculus is the backbone of finance and comes up almost everywhere. Other areas include numerical optimization, numerical interpolation, and numerical linear algebra. Nimit says more firms are going deep into machine learning, and some have set up research arms doing LLM-type work.
Nimit says quants keep finding new fields of math to apply, partly for fun. Still, stochastic calculus is the most unifying part, which Nimit calls finance 101 math.
followups.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.question: How do quants and software engineers collaborate?
answer: Nimit says it depends on the company. At Jane Street, the number of people called quants is small, and traders are technical and implement much of their own work. At Citadel, which Nimit calls more quant-forward, quants may be roughly equal in number to the technical staff. Roles overlap a lot across quants, software engineers, and traders.

At some firms, quants design strategies and hand them to engineers to build. At others, one person may do both, because the person who can implement something best understands its reasons and edge cases. Nimit did a lot of coding, mostly in C++ and some Python.
blocks.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.question: How do finance and tech compare across these roles?
answer: Nimit says the skill set is quite similar. Math and computer science were Nimit's main interests, and the goal was a job that used both. Nimit knew nothing about finance before joining Citadel Securities but read a few recommended textbooks, and technical skill carried the rest. Nimit says AI research works the same way: strong fundamentals let a person pick up the rest.

Nimit says the transition was not rough in either direction. Culture differs, such as San Francisco versus New York, and so do hours. Nimit says quant offers better work-life balance than AI, because AI is very competitive and many places gain an edge by outworking rivals.
blocks.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.question: How are compensation and bonuses structured at quant firms?
answer: Nimit says quant pay has no standard levels like tech companies use. Pay depends on how the firm and the team did that year, how a person's strategies performed if they work on alpha, and seniority or tenure. Nimit says quant firms are secretive, so how these factors combine is opaque. Alpha roles can be very bonus-driven and riskier, while back-office roles tend to be more predictable.
Nimit says multimillion-dollar pay is real for some people, but for the median case pay is still very good, not outlandish.

followups.question: What about NDAs, non-competes, and garden leave?
answer: Nimit says finance firms take confidentiality very seriously. What surprised Nimit, compared with tech, was how tight-lipped people are even within one firm. Teams may have rules on what they can share, and some people stay quiet to protect their alpha.

A non-compete bars a person from working for a competitor for a set period after leaving. The firm usually sets the length. Nimit says it can be zero, up to about two years, and rarely three, with six months to two years as the norm. During that period, called garden leave, the person is paid to not work. It keeps ideas from reaching competitors, and by the time it ends, a strategy may no longer matter.
followups.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

followups.question: Does that secrecy push colleagues to be hostile to one another?
answer: Nimit says the incentive exists. Many people are reluctant, or forbidden, to discuss what they do, and some will not name their sector. Some firms run pods, where each pod is responsible for its own profit and loss and the firm takes a cut.

Pods can end up working on similar ideas without knowing it, since they do not share information. Nimit says the logic is uncorrelated returns. If pods shared ideas, they could converge on similar trades, so one error could wipe out a whole team. Independent work carries less risk.
followups.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.question: What sets the top 1 percent of AI researchers and quants apart?
answer: Nimit says there are several paths. Raw technical skill, intuition, and execution speed all matter. So does playing the political game, which can help people rise. Quant is harder to game because performance is easier to measure. A strong alpha quant who makes the firm a lot of money is clearly recognized.

In AI, the measure is harder to read. A seminal paper or a real breakthrough, such as a much better model, plays the same role. Nimit adds that being in the right place at the right time matters in both fields.
blocks.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.question: What are the top quant firms, and why?
answer: Nimit calls RenTech the gold standard, depending on who you ask, and says its returns over 20 to 30 years are remarkable. Nimit names Jane Street, Citadel, Jump Trading, and Hudson River as other well-regarded firms with strong technical talent and returns. Having one on a resume can help with later quant roles.
Nimit also points to smaller, more secretive firms with excellent returns, naming TGS, in Southern California, plus XTX and Radix as newer firms in that group.
blocks.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.question: Are there any interesting stories from working in quant finance?
answer: Nimit says firms take the rules seriously. Quants face trading restrictions and must get trades pre-approved. Nimit describes stories of people who shared stock tips in group chats and split the profits. That is illegal, and those caught can be fired, sued, or even jailed.

followups.question: Did you see colleagues disappear suddenly?
answer: Nimit says that does happen. Trading on group tips is one of the things firms cover in training. Non-compete disputes can also lead to accusations that someone took strategies to a rival.

Nimit describes job security in quant as an inverse parabola rather than a U shape. Senior quants become expensive, so even a good one can stop being worth the cost, while earlier-career quants cost less. Quant culture is up-or-out and trims low performers. Alpha roles are easy to judge by profit, and trading roles are easy to monitor, so the pressure can be brutal.
followups.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.question: Why did you leave Citadel to join Cartesia?
answer: Nimit says joining Citadel Securities was partly a chance to learn a new domain and finance, and Nimit became more financially literate. By the time Nimit left, growth had started to level off. Nimit had also seen AI take off, having graduated just before ChatGPT came out.

Nimit knew the Cartesia founders from the Stanford PhD and had great respect for their research. A small startup offered growth, a return to AI, and a chance to shape the company and culture as an early employee. Nimit describes this as a different risk profile: after the PhD, Nimit was more risk-averse, but by then had some stability.
blocks.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.question: What problem is Cartesia solving?
answer: Nimit says Cartesia is a voice AI company whose mission is to build the next generation of voice AI and a platform for it. The flagship product is text to speech. Cartesia also offers speech to text and voice agents. Nimit says voice AI is one of the fastest-growing areas of AI, used in call centers, entertainment, and companion products.

followups.question: Why does Cartesia focus on voice?
answer: Nimit says voice is a useful test bed for research ideas. Cartesia has a research arm on longer-term problems such as long context, multimodality, continual learning, memory, and test-time compute. The broader goal is real-time systems that are truly intelligent, that people can interact with, and that learn from experience, such as an always-on personal assistant.
followups.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.question: Who are the top competitors in voice AI?
answer: Nimit names Eleven Labs as the main competitor, a very similar company that Nimit says had about an 18-month head start. Nimit once used Eleven Labs for fun videos, long before Cartesia existed. Nimit says Cartesia stands out for low latency, because a pause between turns of a conversation breaks the illusion of talking to a person.

Nimit also describes the usual voice agent pipeline of speech to text, then a language model, then text to speech. Nimit says this loses information and adds delay, so Cartesia is working toward more end-to-end systems.

followups.question: What would it look like if Cartesia completely beat Eleven Labs?
answer: Nimit says Cartesia already wins on latency and cost. A full win would need quality on many dimensions: following the transcript exactly, which is hard with special characters and repetitions; naturalness; speed; voice cloning; accent localization; and control over emotion. Nimit says Cartesia leads in some areas, trails in others, and wants to lead in as many as possible.

Nimit says switching costs exist in AI, especially with large enterprise customers, though a startup can move faster. If a provider is conclusively better in every way, Nimit says it becomes hard to argue against switching.
followups.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.question: What is the main difference between an AI startup and a big lab?
answer: Nimit says big labs have strong resources, compute, and many researchers. The flip side is that they can be averse to out-of-the-box ideas, prone to groupthink, and less willing to take risks, because failed experiments are expensive. Startups can be more nimble and explore strategically, challenging orthodoxy. That is what drew Nimit to Cartesia.

Nimit credits co-founder Albert Gu with showing, through Mamba, that the common belief that scale alone solves sequence modeling was wrong. Nimit says the work showed real gains in efficiency and quality from state space models, and from hybrids that mix them with transformer layers.

followups.question: Can you give a quick primer on state space models versus transformers?
answer: Nimit says the main challenge of transformers is memory at inference time. Transformers store a representation of every token in a key-value cache, so memory grows linearly with sequence length. For very long sequences, this becomes costly in compute and memory.

State space models compress the past into a state of fixed size, so the cost of each step does not grow with sequence length. Nimit cites co-founder Albert Gu's analogy: a state space model is like a brain with a fixed-size state, while a transformer is more like a database that can recall anything in context. Nimit sees the two as complementary.
followups.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

followups.question: Is the compressed state lossy, and what are the trade-offs?
answer: Nimit says there are trade-offs. On recall-heavy or fact-based tasks, pure state space models can lag transformers, because transformers can do exact in-context recall. On other tasks, state space models can scale as well as or better than transformers, even on a fixed parameter budget.

Nimit says the best of both worlds is often a hybrid that interleaves state space and transformer layers in some ratio. NVIDIA has released work like this, and some recent model families use the same approach. Nimit thinks hybrids are the likely direction for text.

For audio, Nimit says compression is a useful built-in assumption, since each audio frame carries little information. Nimit says state space models improved quality and inference speed in Cartesia's audio work.
followups.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

followups.question: So lossiness is an asset when the data is redundant?
answer: Nimit agrees. Text is densely informational, so each token matters, while audio frames are redundant. Nimit says architecture and data are closely linked, so an architecture cannot be chosen apart from its modality. Co-designing architecture around modality is one of the core research problems that drives Cartesia's work.
followups.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.question: Which works better, a company focused on product or one focused on research?
answer: Nimit says a company should have both. Nimit is skeptical of startups that focus on core research without a clear path to a product. Big labs have more resources, and a company must eventually deliver large returns, so that bet can be all or nothing.

Nimit also sees risk in product-only companies built on other people's models. Many wrapper companies were made obsolete when base models improved enough to do the same work with little scaffolding. Being at the intersection is valuable. A real product shows the issues firsthand, and that drives fixes at the model level, so the company keeps control over its models.
Nimit says Cartesia is first and foremost a product company, and believes building the best products requires solving some fundamental research problems.
blocks.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.question: What advice do you have for a technical person who wants to move into AI research? A host says a software engineer friend worries that software engineering may fade within ten years.
answer: Nimit's philosophy is to build technical skills as much as possible. Once fundamentals are good enough, opportunities tend to come to you. Nimit advises getting as good as possible at coding and AI, reading many papers, and building math skills and intuition, which Nimit has optimized for since undergrad.

Nimit says switching teams or companies can be the only route at a big company, where people can get siloed. Some companies handle moves better, and Nimit has seen engineers move into research. A qualification such as a master's in AI can help with a lateral change.

followups.question: So there are two common paths: more education, or a startup where you mold yourself into a research role?
answer: Nimit says that is roughly right, but even at a startup, a person needs some evidence of the skill, whether grown organically or gained in school. A track record on a resume makes it easier to get a foot in the door. Cartesia has seen people make that switch, because a small company means everyone knows everyone and can judge a change of career from working together.
followups.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.question: What is your biggest regret looking back on your career?
answer: Nimit says they often overthink things and have spent time regretting past decisions that did not matter in the end. Nimit now tries to learn from that and not sweat the small stuff. Minor setbacks happen, and beating oneself up is not a productive use of time.
blocks.speaker: Nimit Sohoni

blocks.question: If you could give your younger self advice on entering the industry, what would it be?
answer: Nimit says to focus on building deep technical skills and not to waste time on trivial work or spread too thin. Focus on the skills you want to use in your day job, get good at them, and spend most of your work time there.
Nimit calls this a simple recipe that is very hard to follow, since it takes discipline, much like exercise and healthy eating.
blocks.speaker: Nimit Sohoni
